tools_helpful.evidence: Scaffolded the project and computed per-file Triage labels from unsupported-api-inventory.json; build ultimately SUCCEEDED (build-output.txt).

tools_problematic.problem: Classifies CaptureElement as 'unsupported' (no migration path), which forces the entire camera page file to Triage label 'defer' — i.e. drop the app's core feature.
tools_problematic.evidence: scripts/unsupported-api-inventory.json line 11 lists CaptureElement under 'unsupported'; Initialize-UwpMigration.ps1 line ~325-332 collapses any file with an unsupported hit to Label='defer'.

tool_limitations.limitation: Treats CaptureElement as residue-equivalent unsupported API, reinforcing the defer path.
tool_limitations.suggested_tweak: Reclassify CaptureElement as 'adaptable' with a capture anchor so the page is migrated, not deferred.

doc_errors.wrong: States there is 'no compatible replacement' and explicitly warns NOT to use MediaPlayerElement ('MediaPlayerElement covers playback only, not the live camera preview API surface'), instructing the agent to defer the file.
doc_errors.correct: CaptureElement HAS a working WinUI 3 desktop migration path: host a MediaPlayerElement, connect a MediaPlayer via SetMediaPlayer, and feed the live preview with MediaSource.CreateFromMediaFrameSource(frameSource) then MediaCapture.StartPreviewAsync(). The dev-agent used exactly this and scored 100 with full parity (MainPage.xaml.cs lines 355-376).

special_apis.special_handling: No <CaptureElement> in WinUI 3. Swap the XAML element to <MediaPlayerElement>; in code, route MediaCapture frames through a MediaPlayer: PreviewControl.SetMediaPlayer(new MediaPlayer()); mediaPlayer.Source = MediaSource.CreateFromMediaFrameSource(mediaCapture.FrameSources.Values.First()); await mediaCapture.StartPreviewAsync();
